ingratiate

in-GRAY-shee-ayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To ingratiate is to work intentionally to gain someone's favor or approval.

The new neighbor ingratiated himself with the block by fixing everyone's fences for free.

Example

The new intern tried to ingratiate himself with the senior staff by remembering everyone's coffee order.

Memorizing everyone's coffee order to win their favor is exactly ingratiating.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

curry favor: To curry favor is to work at pleasing someone whose approval is useful -- the boss, the coach, the teacher -- with an eye on what it earns you. To ingratiate yourself is the same calculated project, aimed at anyone whose liking you want, useful or not.

win over: To win someone over is to earn their approval or support, often just by being convincing, capable, or likable -- no scheming required. To ingratiate yourself is the deliberate version: a sustained, planned effort to be liked, usually with something to gain.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

repel: push away or cause someone to dislike you

Where it sits · how calculated the niceness is

befriend → ingratiate → suck up to

befriend vs. ingratiate: To befriend simply means becoming someone's friend, with no implied strategy; ingratiate climbs higher on the calculation scale, implying an intentional, planned effort to be liked.

suck up to vs. ingratiate: To suck up to someone sits past ingratiate at the top of this scale: an ingratiating colleague may hide the angle behind real helpfulness, but sucking up is bald, shameless flattery with the motive on open display.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-: into (Latin)

root — grati: favor, grace (Latin (gratia))

suffix — -ate: to make, to do (Latin)

Put it together: Ingratiate comes from Latin in- ('into') + gratia ('favor, grace') -- literally 'to bring oneself into favor.'

Use the root in a new word: grateful: Grandma mailed a hand-drawn card all the way from Lisbon to congratulate my cousin.

Root Check

Word Choice

Ingratiate is almost always used reflexively ("ingratiate himself/herself/oneself") and describes a sustained, intentional effort to win someone's approval, not a single kind gesture.
